Carter Holt did not collapse the innings, but he could not free it either, and when Dominic Hale had him stumped, Eastshore were three down with the innings still not fully formed. His 64 was not the fastest innings of the day and not the most violent, but it was the one that made every later Eastshore contribution possible. He started by simply refusing to let Granite turn three wickets into a complete squeeze, playing straight, taking the easy single, and making the bowlers work through longer spells without the reward of another sudden mistake. Evan Marsh then became the partner who let that control turn into a real platform. Evan did not need to dominate. His 44 from 60 carried the right kind of restraint, enough rotation to keep the partnership alive, enough discipline to survive Granite’s tighter overs, and enough scoring sense to stop Dylan from having to manufacture every shift in momentum alone. Their stand was the spine of the innings, lifting Eastshore from a fragile middle point into a position of authority. What made it damaging was not just the runs, it was the time it consumed and the pressure it reversed. Granite had bowlers doing decent work: Cameron had already made two breakthroughs, Dominic was keeping the batters honest, and Finley Cross was beginning to find the sort of rhythm that would later bring wickets. When Finley Cross finally bowled Dylan, Eastshore had already moved into a much safer part of the game. Granite then threatened to drag the score down again. Julian Brooks went quickly, Evan followed soon after, and Felix Grant’s short stay ended before he could turn his boundary into a proper cameo. His 22 had more intent than most of the later hands, and with Dorian still holding the innings together, the pair added the best stand of the card. That passage was important because it took Coastmere beyond the early danger and gave them a route toward a total around two hundred if somebody could stay. Adrian Hale stopped that route from opening. His first major intervention was the wicket of Dorian Ward for 49, a dismissal that mattered far beyond the raw number because Dorian had been the only batter joining the first phase, the repair phase, and the middle overs into one coherent thread. Once he fell, Coastmere were still alive, but they no longer had a true anchor. Elliot Moss followed soon after, pinned in front by the same bowler, and from that point the innings became a sequence of smaller resistance attempts rather than a structure. Mason Reed tried to hold the lower middle together, but he was constantly forced to start again with new partners. Caleb Frost was stumped, Finley Marsh was taken by Adrian Hale in his own follow-through, Gavin Holt was cut off by Logan Price, and even when Connor Hayes and Isaac Dunn dragged the innings into the final overs, it felt more like survival than late acceleration. The total had effort in it, especially from Dorian Ward and from the late Isaac-Connor occupation, but it also carried the clear mark of Adrian Hale’s spell. His five wickets did not arrive as cheap tail-end decoration. He removed the central batter, the one promising middle-order partner, and then several of the pieces Coastmere needed to stretch the innings. Isaac Vale’s ten-over spell was just as important in a quieter way, because three maidens and only 21 conceded kept the middle overs tight enough that Coastmere never had the freedom to rebuild aggressively. Logan Price took two late wickets despite being the more expensive option, Finley Cross gave the first breakthrough, and Dorian Vale closed the innings. Adrian Hale refused to let that happen. He came in after the first-ball shock and batted as if the match needed to be simplified immediately, not through wild hitting, but through controlled aggression. Cameron Blake gave him the right partner: slow enough to stabilize, solid enough to prevent Coastmere from attacking only one end, and calm enough to let Adrian keep the tempo high. Their partnership of 93 essentially broke the chase open. Adrian’s 66 from 47 was the innings that erased Coastmere’s best chance of turning 166 into a nervous defence. He hit strongly square, drove cleanly when the ball was overpitched, and used the boundary options early enough that the field had to spread before Coastmere had created real scoreboard pressure. Cameron’s 26 looked modest next to that, but it was structurally vital because it kept the chase from becoming dependent on one batter. Gavin Holt eventually removed Adrian, and that wicket gave Coastmere a way back into the emotional side of the game even if the equation had already become much easier. He then took Cameron as well, and when Liam Parker’s brisk 22 ended after a short burst of hitting, the chase began to wobble more than Ridgefield would have wanted. Dorian Vale and Hayden Marsh added enough to keep the score moving, but Gavin Holt kept dragging the game back, having Hayden stumped and then watching Dorian run out immediately after, leaving the chase suddenly less clean. Isaac Vale was then bowled by Gavin Holt, and from a position that had looked almost routine, Ridgefield had slipped to seven down with a small but real amount still to finish. That is why the final partnership mattered. Finley Cross did not need to play a grand hand. He needed to stay. Noah Bennett, by contrast, needed only a few balls to close the argument, and he did it with exactly the right clarity, striking three boundaries in a short unbeaten burst and removing any lingering doubt before Coastmere could turn wickets into true panic. Ridgefield reached 169 for 7 in the twenty-seventh over and won by three wickets, a result that looked slightly tense at the end but was still rooted in the Adrian Hale passage much earlier.
